explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, friend, but the text says something else. The Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, hears Israel is coming along the road to Atharim, and he attacks Israel (Numbers 21:1). No welcome mat, no wave from the porch. He picks a fight and takes some prisoners.

That's it, baker! The king of Arad doesn't let anybody pass in peace. The text says he hears Israel is coming along the road to Atharim, and he attacks Israel (Numbers 21:1). He's a Canaanite king who lived in the Negev, and his answer to company is a fight.

Right on the money, baker. The text says the king of Arad attacked Israel "and captured some prisoners." That's all it tells us he took. Real people were taken, and I think that's why the next part matters so much.

Good guess, since attackers grabbing treasure is a common story. But this passage doesn't mention any gold or silver. It says the king attacked Israel "and captured some prisoners." People were taken, not treasure.

I can see how you got there, friend. Flocks and herds are a big deal in a lot of Bible stories. Here, though, the text says the king of Arad attacked Israel "and captured some prisoners." It doesn't say a word about animals.

explanations.answer: They make a vow to the LORD
explanations.explanation: YES, baker! After the attack, Israel "made a vow to the LORD" (Numbers 21:2). They took it straight to Him. Me, I'd have been busy rearranging the takeout menus.

explanations.answer: They build an altar to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Altars do show up all over the Bible, so that's a fair guess. But this passage never says Israel builds one. What it says is that Israel "made a vow to the LORD" (Numbers 21:2). They spoke straight to Him with a promise.

Spies are a classic move, friend, and Israel does send spies in other places. Not here, though. After the attack, the text says Israel "made a vow to the LORD" (Numbers 21:2). Their first move is a promise, with no scouting trip.

explanations.answer: Hand the people of Arad over to them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Israel says, "If You will deliver this people into our hands…" (Numbers 21:2). They're asking the LORD to give them this people. And notice they ask Him, not anybody else.

explanations.answer: Give them a safe road past Arad
explanations.explanation: A safe road sounds sensible, friend, especially with prisoners already taken. But that's not what Israel asks. Their vow says, "If You will deliver this people into our hands…" (Numbers 21:2). They ask for the people of Arad to be delivered to them, not for a way around.

explanations.answer: Lead them far away from the Negev
explanations.explanation: Running for the hills is what I'd have asked for, baker! But Israel asks for something different. Their vow says, "If You will deliver this people into our hands…" (Numbers 21:2). They don't ask to leave. They ask for the LORD to deliver these people to them.
That's right, baker. The text says, "the LORD heard Israel's plea and delivered up the Canaanites" (Numbers 21:3). Israel asked, and the LORD heard it. That plea went somewhere.
Not this time, friend. Numbers 21:3 says, "And the LORD heard Israel's plea and delivered up the Canaanites." So the LORD does deliver them up. He heard the plea, and the text says what He did.
You got it, baker! The text says, "Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction" (Numbers 21:3). That's exactly what they vowed in verse 2. They said it, and then they did it.

That's a fair worry, since promises get broken all the time. I've promised to eat just one cookie more than once. But Israel doesn't break this one. The text says, "Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction" (Numbers 21:3), which is what they vowed.

Putting things off is very human, friend. I've got a drawer full of years that could vouch for me. But the text doesn't show Israel waiting. It says the LORD delivered up the Canaanites, and "Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction" (Numbers 21:3).
Perfect, baker! The text says, "so they named the place Hormah" (Numbers 21:3). That's the name the passage ends on, and it's the title of this whole lesson.
Meribah is a real place name in the Bible, so that was a smart pick, friend. But it's not the one here. In this passage, Israel names the place Hormah (Numbers 21:3).
Kadesh is a real place in the Bible too, so I see where that came from. But in this passage, it's not the name Israel gives. The text says, "so they named the place Hormah" (Numbers 21:3).
